items.title: Lionsgate kept ‘The Hunger Games’ opposite GTA VI’s launch. That paid off with a $120 million opening

Hollywood had reason to worry that young audiences would spend the weekend at home, with gamers taking time off from work, stocking up on pizza rolls, and clearing their schedules for Grand Theft Auto VI. But while millions of players were busy exploring the game’s virtual world, moviegoers were making their way to Panem, handing The Hunger Games a $120 million domestic opening as GTA VI set records of its own.

Lionsgate had considered the risks of releasing the film opposite GTA VI before deciding to stick with its date, according to the Associated Press , and the gamble appears to have paid off. But that bet held up in part because the movie and the game weren’t chasing quite the same audience.

Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to $120 million in North America and $225 million worldwide, according to the studio’s Sunday estimates, according to the AP. It was the franchise’s biggest opening in more than a decade, arriving the day after the long-awaited release of GTA VI, which Rockstar Games estimates generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales on its first day.

Some 74% of The Hunger Games opening-weekend audience was between 18 and 34 years old, according to the Associated Press , including Gen Z and younger millennials who have plenty of entertainment options at home but are still willing to turn out for the right movie. 

Still, the weekend wasn’t necessarily a case of gamers putting down their controllers and picking up a bucket of popcorn. Women accounted for 67% of The Hunger Games audience, according to opening-weekend polling,…
items.t: Lionsgate kept ‘The Hunger Games’ opposite GTA VI’s launch. That paid off with a $120 million opening

items.title: Nvidia’s board ousted Jensen Huang for a ‘lack of candor.’ Twelve days later, the same directors brought him back
items.summary:
Business history was made today, and none of it will be remembered with pride. Less than two weeks ago, on Nov. 11, Jensen Huang stepped down under pressure from his board, which accepted his resignation. Six days later, chair Harvey Jones declared that the board “does not intend to reinstate” the founder and rebuffed his offer to return. The following day, Jones informed employees that directors had acted over personal conduct and a “lack of candor.” Today, those same directors voted unanimously to bring him back, saying they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor.”

Rarely in American business have directors removed a chief executive over graver allegations. Huang misled his board about personal relationships, including one with the leader of a major customer whom U.S. officials suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. A national security inquiry is underway , alongside Reuters and Bloomberg reports that restricted chips were smuggled into China and reached military buyers. Meanwhile, the SEC is examining Nvidia’s accounting. Directors reversed course anyway, acting before their investigators could finish the work.

In our forthcoming book , When Machines Act: The Promise and Peril of Our Agentic AI Future (MIT Press/Penguin Random House), we draw directly on Huang’s commentary from our Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute CEO forums, making this breakdown in corporate oversight all the more sobering.

Fired, Rehired, and What It Usually Means 

Some founders have earned a second act. Apple forced Steve Jobs out in 1985 after he went to war against his…
items.t: Nvidia’s board ousted Jensen Huang for a ‘lack of candor.’ Twelve days later, the same directors brought him back

items.title: Prediction markets put Jensen Huang’s odds of returning at 11% on Sunday night—hours later he was back as Nvidia CEO
items.summary:
Prediction markets have proved prescient when it comes to forecasting elections and other events, but in the case of Jensen Huang’s abrupt return as Nvidia’s CEO, they appeared as much in the dark as everyone else. A look at contracts on Kalshi and Polymarket tied to the company’s next CEO reveals an abrupt swing from long shots to near certainties when the board reinstated him Monday morning.

One Kalshi contract on whether Nvidia’s next CEO would be an internal or external hire drew nearly $100,000 in trading volume. At 5 a.m., traders gave an external hire roughly 57% odds and an internal one roughly 33%. A third option, that Huang would return, was trading at about 16% before the news broke. Traders then piled in, and it jumped to nearly 100% within minutes. 

Another contract, on whether President Donald Trump would publicly call for Huang’s reinstatement, drew more than $330,000 in volume. Bettors gave it a 38% chance of happening before January 2027 and a 20% chance before December 2026. They were wrong on both counts. Trump made such a post on Truth Social on Sunday night, and the contract was resolved. The odds for the January window jumped to 83% and those for the December window to 74%. Because the call came before December, both contracts paid out on “yes.”

Polymarket saw even heavier trading. A contract on who would be Nvidia’s next CEO topped $11 million in volume. As of Sunday evening, Nvidia insider Ian Buck led with roughly 13%, followed by Huang at roughly 11%, with finance chief Colette Kress and former Apple CEO Tim Cook trailing. By early Monday…
items.t: Prediction markets put Jensen Huang’s odds of returning at 11% on Sunday night—hours later he was back as Nvidia CEO

items.title: ‘Totally involved’: Trump says ‘I convinced’ Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang
items.summary:
The White House is taking credit for putting Jensen Huang back in charge of Nvidia .

“President Trump was totally involved, and this is a great decision by the Nvidia board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Fortune .

But that’s just the White House; the president is saying he was the one to persuade the board to bring him back.

“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” he told CNBC’s Eamon Javers in a phone interview Monday.

“And I convinced them.”

Nvidia announced Monday that Huang is again its president, CEO, and board member. The company said directors voted unanimously after input from senior levels of the U.S. government left them confident his return poses no national security risk. The board reportedly met late Sunday night, just as the president posted hours earlier that he hoped the board would rehire Huang.

On CNBC, he said directors “did ask for assurance on the national security threat.”

“And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot,” Trump said. The president did not say whether he dialed into the meeting himself, but he did say he was “represented” there.

“I’m very, very happy that the company had the courage, and the board had the courage, to do the right thing, and they suffered for two weeks, and the company suffered greatly,” the president told CNBC.

Statesman or shareholder? 

Trump in recent days had said he would like to see the return of Huang to Nvidia, adding that the former CEO “did nothing wrong.”

“People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s…

items.title: Nvidia board votes unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang after deciding he ‘poses no national security risk’
items.summary:
Nvidia’s board has voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO effective immediately, the company said on Monday, stating that the cofounder of the world’s dominant AI chipmaker poses no national security risk. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago after reports emerged about a series of affairs, one with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese asset.

“The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” board chair Harvey C. Jones said in the statement that came just days after Jones insisted on Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call that the board did not intend to bring Huang back . 

“In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the company said on Monday.

Nvidia stock rose 29% immediately prior to the opening bell in New York, and was up roughly 34% in midday trading, sparking a market-wide rally that lifted the S&P 500 by 5%, the Dow Jones industrial average by 6.8%, and the Nasdaq by 3.2%.

The move marks a stunning U-turn by Nvidia’s board and follows a sharp selloff in Nvidia stock last week that also hit the broader AI trade. Huang has also been one of the AI industry’s most influential boosters, and some investors had worried that without Huang, some of Nvidia’s investments and support of the wider ecosystem could weaken or collapse. items.title: Morgan Freeman says AI should do ‘what we actually are dreaming of doing’—but deepfakes have also made him say things he never said
items.summary:
Morgan Freeman has arguably the most recognizable voice in Hollywood—and that’s made him a frequent target for AI copycats.

“You can create artists and make them say things they never said, which has happened to me,” Freeman told Fortune . 

Freeman isn’t against the technology itself. He and longtime producing partner Lori McCreary have spent decades putting new tools to work in filmmaking through their movie production company, Revelations Entertainment. The issue, he said, is privacy.

“What we should be doing with technology is what we actually are dreaming of doing,” he said. “But we have to somehow protect privacy, and that’s the first thing that loses its grip.”

McCreary, who cofounded Revelations Entertainment with Freeman in 1996, said AI is different from the tools that came before it. About two and a half years ago, she came across a clip online she didn’t remember Freeman filming, so she called to ask him about it. 

“He was like, ‘I don’t remember.’ And that was the first time when I thought, ‘Okay, we’ve got to get ahead of this,’” McCreary told Fortune .

Freeman has pushed back about AI copies of his voice, too. Last November, Freeman told the Guardian that his lawyers had been “very, very busy” and had found “quite a few” instances of his voice being replicated without his consent. And in June 2024, he also thanked fans on X for calling out unauthorized AI imitations of his voice. 

McCreary said they now get calls every day about people using Freeman’s voice to sell products online that he has no connection to. AI can reproduce his voice and his…
items.t: Morgan Freeman says AI should do ‘what we actually are dreaming of doing’—but deepfakes have also made him say things he never said

items.title: After the Palisades fire, a founder built AI to help survivors with paperwork. Now he needs a state to buy it
items.summary:
When the Palisades fire tore through his Los Angeles neighborhood in January 2025, Jonathon Nostrant’s house was damaged but still standing. Many of his neighbors’ homes were destroyed.

The fire was only the first ordeal. Next, Nostrant encountered a tangle of federal, state, and local assistance programs, each with its own forms, eligibility rules, and deadlines. Survivors with insurance must also report their payouts to every agency they apply to, because FEMA cannot pay for losses an insurer already covers. 

Insurance was already a sore subject in the Palisades. A year before the fire, State Farm dropped roughly 1,600 policies in the neighborhood, Fortune reported as the fire burned .

“Our insurance was fighting with us,” Nostrant said in an interview, describing his own claim.

That experience led to AidFinder, a Miami-based startup Nostrant cofounded that uses AI to match disaster survivors with programs they may qualify for, explain eligibility rules, and prepare applications. Survivors review everything before submission. The intended customers, though, are states, which would offer the platform to residents under their own banner.

For now, it is a pitch. AidFinder hasn’t signed its first state customer, and survivors have yet to use the platform, Refresh Miami reported on Nov. 17 . Nostrant told the outlet the company is in talks with 30 states, including Florida, and that Craig Fugate, who ran FEMA under President Barack Obama, has accepted a seat on its board.

A voice-tech veteran takes on paperwork 

Nostrant has spent much of his career teaching machines…

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…

items.title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
items.summary:
PM challenges rivals to rebuff plan he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope

Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”

This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage
items.t: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
